extracted.intended_audience: writers, screenwriters, and storytellers (esp. those interested in narrative structure, manga/anime creators, and narrative theory readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and applying the kishōtenketsu four-part narrative structure (Ki, Shō, Ten, Ketsu) as an alternative paradigm to Western three-act plotting, with guidance on function, pacing, and examples from manga/anime screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ki 起 — Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening segment that introduces characters, situation, and the hook; it establishes expectations. In the post: Ki is supposed to take roughly 10–15% of the length of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ki to set up the protagonist and key devices (example: Itadori and the talisman in Jujutsu Kaisen). This is often short relative to the rest of the story and prepares the audience's expectations which the later Ten will act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shō 承 — Development
rubrics_metrics.description: The long development segment where the main story unfolds and the primary expectations are set; described as the longest part of the four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shō is where the main conflict/emergent problem appears and expectations about how events will proceed are built (example: Fushiguro warning Itadori about the talisman). The blog cites ~60% of story length as an illustrative proportion for Shō.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten 転 — Twist
rubrics_metrics.description: The twist segment whose role is to defy audience expectations; Ten functions relative to what the audience already anticipates and is based on the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design Ten to subvert or surprise in a way that reframes prior events rather than simply serving as a Western-style midpoint or plot-point. The effectiveness of Ten depends on previously established expectations in Ki/Shō.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ketsu 結 — Conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The concluding segment in which reader attention and plot tension typically fall away; Ketsu is not usually the place for a Western-style climax but for resolution and balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ketsu often shows calm after Ten, reveals character motivations/growth, and restores a new equilibrium (example: the calm after the fight in Jujutsu Kaisen). The author notes Ketsu may occupy roughly the final ~10% and that cliffhangers or epilogues may follow outside the proper Ketsu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing defined by audience emotional engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu is defined by the effect of events on the audience (reader’s emotional engagement curve) rather than strictly by character/plot beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan act lengths and beats with how they move reader attention: Ki and Ketsu can be short and lighter in dramatic weight while Shō occupies the core of engagement. Use an engagement curve to pace the story rather than translating Western plot-point timing directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation setup then subversion as core mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: The central operating principle is to set up expectations (in Ki/Shō) and then act upon/subvert them in Ten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft earlier segments to create specific audience assumptions that Ten can meaningfully defy. The twist must relate to those assumptions to be effective; mere randomness will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict is not the defining requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike Western three-act structures that foreground conflict, kishōtenketsu does not require a clearly defined conflict as its core; focus is on expectation and pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force a Western-style antagonistic conflict if the story's logic relies on situational contrast and surprise. That said, the author cautions that kishōtenketsu is not strictly conflict-less—conflict can appear but is not the organizing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical proportional guidance for the four acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested rough proportions: Ki ~10–15% of story, Shō ~60% (the longest), Ketsu ~10% (with Ten occupying the pivoting portion between development and conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proportions come from the mangaka-diagram and the Jujutsu Kaisen episode example; use them as flexible guides rather than rigid rules. Mapping scenes to minutes (the post references specific minute marks) can help test proportional fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across media and scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishōtenketsu is used across children’s stories, serial manga, anime, film (Kurosawa cited), and even non-narrative media like PowerPoint presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may apply the four-part logic at macro (whole work) or micro (single episode/scene) levels. The post analyses a single anime episode as a micro-version of the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation/translation caution versus three-act models
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate kishōtenketsu to a simple 3-act structure with an added midpoint; Ki and Ketsu have different dramatic weight and the paradigm emphasizes audience/pace over plot points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literal translation traps (e.g., assuming 'no conflict' means 'no drama'). Treat kishōtenketsu as an alternate paradigm focused on different evaluative elements (audience effect and tempo) rather than as a direct mapping onto Western plot-points.
